01

Film Poster Conventions

Film posters are a form of promotion — seen on billboards, bus stops, buses, underground stations and around cinemas. You need the conventions cold: they're the backbone of every media language answer.

Types of poster

  • TEASER poster — released well before the film to generate hype and "whet appetites". Gives away little about the plot; often no release date (things may still change). NTTD's teaser: Bond alone, rifle raised, no date beyond a month.
  • MAIN poster — a dominant image (key signifier) or montage of characters, with more key information: release date, actors, director, and often a credit block with institutional details (e.g. IMAX). Posters are altered through the campaign to keep audience attention.
  • CHARACTER posters — one per major character, building familiarity and letting fans "collect" the cast.
  • BANNERS — wide formats for billboards and websites.
Teaser
Character
Character
Banner format

The conventions — and how they work

The techniqueHow it works
The pictureHelps the audience understand the genre; may be a still that hints at the narrative.
The taglineGives a sense of genre and tone (comical, fearful…); reused across other products for audience recognition.
Credit blockAll the institutional information — kept small so it doesn't distract.
Star names / star imageAppeal to an existing audience; the star in character is a selling point for fans.
Release dateImportant around key times of year.
Reference to producer/directorRelies on a previous film's reputation to bring in an audience.
EnigmaCreates mystery and questions ("who is the killer?") — the audience must see the film to get answers.

Full checklist: title & typography · tagline · billing block · main focal image · star billing · institution logo · reviews/star ratings · release date · auteur reference.

Bond's own codes & conventions

The franchise has its own repertoire of elements audiences expect: the gun and the 007 gun-barrel logo, the tuxedo, the martini, the Aston Martin, gadgets and the luxury watch, exotic global locations, one-liners, a title song, glamorous "Bond girls", and larger-than-life villains.

These become intertextual hooks — every new poster trades on 60 years of Bond iconography.

02

The Man with the Golden Gun (1974)

Roger Moore's second outing as 007. Learn the poster inch by inch — the exam has asked about its colour [5] and genre conventions [10].

19 Dec 1974
Release date — Roger Moore's 2nd Bond film
$7m → $97m
Budget → worldwide box office. Produced by Eon, distributed by United Artists
Ian Fleming
Based on his novel — author's name appears with the title
McGinnis
Poster artwork by illustrator Robert McGinnis — illustration was standard before the 1990s

Historical context

  • Before the 1990s, illustrations were far more common on film posters — limited technology.
  • Set during the 1973 energy crisis: the oil embargo by oil-producing Arab nations had short- and long-term effects on politics and the economy worldwide — hinted at in the film's solar-energy MacGuffin.
  • To ride the martial arts craze (Bruce Lee, Jackie Chan), the film includes Kung Fu scenes and was filmed mostly in Asia — Hong Kong, Thailand and Macau.

The poster, piece by piece

  • Central image: a mid-shot of Bond, smartly dressed, gun across his body. His dominance suggests he is the protagonist — Propp's hero.
  • Direct address: Bond looks straight at the audience; the intense stare and lack of a smile connote how seriously he expects to be taken — calm despite the chaos around him, the conventional strength of a hero.
  • Costume & props: the attire connotes business and professionalism; the gun — part of Bond's "uniform" — signifies danger and action.
  • Star billing: "ROGER MOORE as JAMES BOND 007" sits directly above Bond's image — Moore was a household name from The Saint and Live and Let Die.
  • The golden gun: an extreme close-up pointed at Bond, being loaded with a bullet engraved with his name — an attempted assassination narrative and an enigma code: whose hand is it? (Propp's villain.)
  • Montage: unconventionally, lots of images — the audience works through them to piece together a complex plot.
  • Credit block small and tucked away; title + Ian Fleming's name at the bottom links to the novels.
The set text — you get a clean copy in the exam
The enigma: a named bullet, an unseen villain
Star billing above the hero

Colour — the 5-marker the exam actually asked

  • The colour of the gun connotes wealth and status; the golden palette is referenced frequently to link with the film's title — and intertextually with Goldfinger, the film that fixed the franchise's conventions.
  • Bond's tuxedo is the darkest colour at the centre of the frame, drawing the eye to the hero.
  • Text at top and bottom shares a consistent palette, linking actor, character and title.
  • The two women's bikinis could connote roles: red = heroine, black = villain.
  • Overall: red, black and orange = action-adventure codes, with silver "laboratory" elements hinting at science fiction.

03

The Narrative Theory Toolkit

Story = the sequence of events (the plot). Narrative = the way those events are put together and told. Four theorists to apply to both posters.

Todorov — 5-stage narrative

  • 1. Equilibrium — everything balanced; a calm, normal start.
  • 2. Disruption — a dramatic event upsets the peace.
  • 3. Recognition — the protagonist realises something is wrong.
  • 4. Repair — the protagonist tries to fix the problem.
  • 5. New equilibrium — balance restored, but with change.

On a poster you infer the stage: NTTD's title even hints at Todorov — "no time to die" suggests a disruption Bond is racing to repair.

Propp — 8 character types

Hero · Villain · Helper · Donor · Princess (+ her Father) · Dispatcher · False hero.

  • TMWTGG: Bond = hero; the unseen hand holding the golden gun = villain; the "Bond women" = conventional princesses needing saving; the kung-fu fighter beside Bond = a helper, perhaps.
  • NTTD: Bond = hero; the masked man with a gun = villain; and crucially, the women refuse the princess role.

Lévi-Strauss — binary oppositions

Meaning is produced through opposites: good vs evil · male vs female · dark vs light · East vs West · humanity vs technology.

On the NTTD poster: warm Italian daylight vs the cold neon of Bar El Nido; hero vs masked villain; the teaser's Bond half in shadow = light vs dark, good vs evil.

Barthes — enigma codes

A text plants a mystery or question the audience needs answered — a cliffhanger, a partial reveal.

TMWTGG: whose hand loads the bullet engraved "007"? NTTD: who is the man in the mask, and why is he hiding his identity?

04

No Time to Die (2021)

The modern set text: a montage main poster for Daniel Craig's final Bond. Assessed for media language and representation in Section A — and industry in Section B.

Media language — semiotic analysis

  • Dominant image: a mid-shot of Bond, smartly dressed — the protagonist, Propp's hero. Action shots of him on a bike and in a car connote he is on a quest.
  • Direct address: Safin (Rami Malek), Q and Swann look straight at the audience — a common poster convention that feels personal.
  • No star names: unusually, actors' names are missing — producers are confident audiences recognise Daniel Craig, and text would detract from the visuals. Visual star appeal instead: Lashana Lynch is recognisable from Captain Marvel.
  • The 007 logo: large and bold at the top; the worn, aged blue tone hints at a more experienced Bond, and coheres with the blues of Bar El Nido, the villain's suit and Paloma's dress.
  • Guns: genre props promising violence, action and danger — each casually pointed, connoting figures alert and ready.
  • Costume contrast: Nomi's military kit and earpiece connote an active 00 agent — calm, focused, in control. Paloma's glamorous, revealing navy dress is the historic "Bond Girl" code.
  • Title block: the gold "007" connotes luxury, wealth, aspiration, exclusivity; the capitalised title suggests power. Below it: release date, social media, production companies and distributors — kept small.
  • Locations: exotic settings (Italy, Cuba) shown in background shots — a Hollywood spy-thriller convention.
The set text — the montage main poster

Intertextuality

  • The montage design — images laid over each other — references previous Bond posters: familiarity, nostalgia and pleasure for fans.
  • The 007 gun logo is an intertextual link across the whole franchise — synonymous with Bond.
  • Significant absence: no reference to Ian Fleming — NTTD is not based on one of his novels, a departure from previous films (compare TMWTGG, where his name sits beside the title).
Goldfinger — the film that fixed the franchise's codes
Montage posters are a Bond tradition — familiarity and nostalgia
Halle Berry as Jinx — people of colour were historically cast as villains or "Bond Girls"

05

Representation — 1974 vs 2021

Two posters, fifty years apart — the perfect study in how representations of gender, ethnicity and age respond to changing contexts.

TMWTGG (1974) — the 70s on a page

Each crop of the poster is an exam point — picture the detail, write the paragraph.

BondCentral, dominant, suited, armed — size and positioning encode power; his direct gaze commands the frame. The stereotypical 1970s man.
The women — narrative rolesOne points at Bond, one drapes an arm across him — defined entirely in relation to the hero. Allies and enemies "all look the same", hard to tell apart.
The women — the male gazeBikini-clad, slim, "perfect hourglass figures and long flowing hair" — highly sexualised, positioned around and below Bond as objects of desire: Propp's princesses, Mulvey's male gaze. Note the colour coding: red bikini = heroine, black = villain.
EthnicityThe kung-fu characters are highlighted by dress and gesture codes — riding the 1970s martial arts trend; the "Asian" woman in a fighting pose is represented differently from the sexualised Western women.
The (near-)unseen villainScaramanga barely features — the golden gun stands in for him: menace via props rather than presence, leaving Bond unchallenged as the poster's only true male power.
IdeologyA patriarchal world where men act and women decorate — reflecting the era, even as second-wave feminism was challenging it. The named bullet aims all the danger at the man who matters.

NTTD (2021) — evolution (with limits)

MasculinityBond appears three times — still the centre. But the main image shows a thoughtful, care-worn expression, and he holds no weapon — atypical for the genre: a more modern, emotionally complex masculinity.
Women — agencyNomi holds her weapon with relaxed confidence; military costume and earpiece make her central to the plot — not a "damsel in distress" or Proppian princess. A Black woman carrying the 007 number is franchise history.
Women — the limitKey lighting and make-up still present all three women as beautiful (the Hollywood expectation), and Paloma's glamorous, revealing dress is the historic "Bond Girl" code surviving into 2021.
Ethnicity — the counter-readingThe cast is still predominantly white. Safin (Rami Malek, of Egyptian heritage) is the second-most dominant figure — villains continue the franchise pattern of "othered" antagonists.
The Noh maskThe masked figure borrows Japanese Noh theatre imagery (used for ghostly, demonic characters) — an enigma code AND another ethnically "othered" threat.
AgeThe lighting deliberately highlights Bond's older, weathered face against a youthful supporting cast — experience vs energy, and a franchise saying goodbye to its star.

Gender balance — the judgement: the two most dominant figures are still male (Bond and Safin) — evolution, yes, but the franchise remains male-driven.

Contexts that shaped NTTD

  • #OscarsSoWhite (2016) and the Black Lives Matter movement following George Floyd's death (2020) pushed Hollywood to re-examine representation of race and ethnicity.
  • The feminist movement and modern audience expectations pushed the franchise beyond the "Bond Girl" — compare Grace Jones, Gloria Hendry, Halle Berry and Naomie Harris on earlier posters.
  • Bond himself has been constructed since the 1960s to embody masculine stereotypes — strength, skill, independence — and the poster continues that even as it softens him.

Sort it: Conform or Challenge? (stereotypes across both posters)

TMWTGG: bikini-clad women positioned around Bond as objects of desire
TMWTGG: Bond central, dominant, armed and suited — power encoded in size and position
NTTD: Bond shown without a weapon, with a thoughtful, care-worn expression
NTTD: Nomi in military costume with an earpiece — an active 00 agent, not a damsel
NTTD: Paloma's glamorous, revealing evening dress — the historic "Bond Girl" code
NTTD: the two most dominant figures on the poster are both male
NTTD: a Black woman carrying the 007 number — a first in franchise history
NTTD: the villains are "othered" — Egyptian heritage actor, Japanese Noh mask

This mix is your top-band argument: NTTD challenges some stereotypes while still upholding others — change, but not a revolution.

06 · Comp 1 Sec B

Industry — Production & the Film Business

Section B asks stepped questions (usually 17 marks: 1 + 2 + 2 + 12) about how No Time to Die was made, funded, distributed and shown. The short answers test facts — so drill them.

30 Sep 2021
UK release — delayed from April 2020 by a director change and the pandemic
25th
Film in the Bond franchise
$250–301m
Budget — one of the most expensive films ever made
$774m+
Grossed worldwide (~£620m)

Key terms — say them in your sleep

  • Budget / funding — how much the film costs to make.
  • Commercial — made to make a profit. Non-commercial — not made for profit.
  • Mass audience — as large an audience as possible. Niche audience — small and specific.
  • Mainstream — made by a big company for a mass audience. Independent — made by a small company, usually for a niche audience.
  • Franchise — a series/collection of related films in succession.
  • High production values — a big budget: lots of action, stunts, CGI, a blockbuster look.

Who made No Time to Die?

  • EON Productions ("Everything Or Nothing") — the British production company that produces the Bond films and co-owns the rights…
  • …with MGM. Amazon bought MGM in 2022, gaining rights to stream the Bond catalogue on Prime Video.
  • Universal Pictures distributed in the UK and internationally; United Artists Releasing distributed in North America.
  • The poster was designed by Empire Designs (a British film promotion agency); the title logo is set in Futura Black; the billing block credits cast, crew, producers and distributors.

The five stages of film production (in order!)

StageWhat happens
1. DevelopmentCreating ideas · buying the rights to a novel/play · writing the screenplay · finding the money.
2. Pre-productionBuilding sets · choosing locations · casting the stars · hiring the crew.
3. ProductionShooting the film.
4. Post-productionEditing · adding sound and visual effects.
5. DistributionMarketing the film · screening at cinemas · DVD/Blu-ray release · streaming.

The industry also splits into three areas: PRODUCTION (the production company makes the film) → DISTRIBUTION (prints + marketing) → EXHIBITION (cinemas pay the distributor and share box office takings on a percentage basis).

Conglomerates, vertical integration & synergy

  • Conglomerate — a large (often multinational) company that owns and controls many smaller companies (subsidiaries). Universal owns companies across film, TV, music — and theme parks.
  • Vertical integration — one company controls more than one stage of production/distribution. Universal both produces and distributes (for NTTD it acted as distributor only — EON produced).
  • Synergy — different parts of a company (or partnered brands) working together. Example: Billie Eilish's theme song was released on Interscope Records — owned by Universal Music Group. One release promotes the film, the song and the label at once.
The theme song: Billie Eilish on Interscope (Universal Music Group) — synergy in action
Amazon bought MGM in 2022 — Bond streams on Prime Video

How did NTTD appeal to a mass audience?

  • An iconic character with universal appeal — charming, but with more emotional depth than earlier Bonds.
  • A familiar, nostalgic narrative — good defeats bad — reinforcing dominant messages about duty and loyalty.
  • Star appeal: Daniel Craig; double-Oscar-winner Christoph Waltz; Oscar-winner Rami Malek; Ralph Fiennes (Voldemort!); Lashana Lynch (Captain Marvel); Ben Whishaw (Paddington's voice).
  • A female scriptwriter — Phoebe Waller-Bridge — giving female characters convincing characterisation and dialogue, appealing to a contemporary (and female) audience.
  • IMAX release — very high resolution on huge screens; perfect for a film of "spectacle" with big action scenes and CGI.
  • High production values — real stunts on a blockbuster budget.
High production values: real stunt work, not just CGI

07 · Comp 1 Sec B

Industry — Regulation (BBFC)

Films in Britain are regulated by the BBFC (British Board of Film Classification), which awards age certificates. A real past-paper opener: "Name the organisation that regulates films in Britain [1]".

The certificates

  • U — universal, suitable for all · PG — parental guidance.
  • 12A — cinema only: under-12s must be with an adult. 12 — home media: no one under 12 may watch. That difference is a classic 2-marker.
  • 15 and 18 — no one younger admitted.

Why NTTD wanted a 12A: to reach the widest possible audience (and maximise profit) while keeping the action, threat and moderate violence Bond audiences expect. Families can attend together — crucial for a mainstream blockbuster.

The NINE things the BBFC considers

  • Bad language
  • Threat and horror (danger and the potential to scare)
  • Dangerous behaviour
  • Drugs
  • Violence
  • Sex
  • Sexual violence and sexual threat
  • Nudity
  • Discrimination (race, gender, religion, disability, sexuality)

For the 12-marker ("Explain why a film may be given a 12A or 12 certificate — refer to NTTD"): why films need regulating · the commercial benefit of a 12A · what is/isn't allowed at 12A · the SPECIFIC content in NTTD (moderate violence, sustained threat, brief strong language) that placed it there.

08 · Comp 1 Sec B

Industry — Marketing, the Website & Convergence

A global brand needs a global campaign. Bond was marketed in a very similar way across the world because the brand image is so strong — and every element links to every other.

Key terms first

Marketing — promoting the film (posters, trailers…)
Brand — a well-known product or company name
Merchandising — products linked to the film (toys, games, posters…)
Promotional partnership (synergy) — companies pay to link their products with the film
Product placement — showing a partner's product IN the film
Technological convergence — technology coming together in one place (your phone: photos, web, social media)

The campaign timeline

  • Teaser poster released on James Bond Day — 5 October 2019 — as part of a global campaign, nearly two years before release: enigma, minimal information.
  • Character posters — one per major character, building star appeal and letting different fans find "their" way in.
  • Theatrical poster + billing block just before release, revealing more narrative.
  • Teaser and theatrical trailers — escalating reveals.
  • Magazine covers — Total Film, Empire, plus men's style magazines like GQ: Bond's sophisticated image matches GQ brands like Tom Ford and Omega — which are also promotional partners. Special subscriber-only covers turned fans into collectors.
  • Royal Premiere — 28 September 2021 at the Royal Albert Hall, with the royals attending — streamed live on YouTube: free global press coverage and prestige.
  • TV chat shows — the stars on Graham Norton, shown as people rather than characters — a different, relatable appeal.
  • Social media & viral content — instant worldwide reach; audiences share and feel part of a fan community; producers get direct feedback.
The Royal Premiere — publicity money can't buy
Chat shows: stars as people
Magazine covers

Land Rover — the 007 Defender. Chopard — 7,007-piece "Golden Hearts" jewellery. Michael Kors — Moneypenny's Bancroft satchel. Bollinger — official champagne for 40+ years. Triumph — its limited-edition 007 bike sold out in the US in 47 seconds. adidas — NTTD UltraBoost trainers hooking a younger demographic. Nokia — the XR20 fronted by Lashana Lynch in character as Nomi. Heineken — the "Worth the Wait" spot with Daniel Craig. Smirnoff — "There's a Spy in Everyone". Swatch — Q's ²Q watch, worn by Ben Whishaw on screen. DHL — official logistics partner since Casino Royale, with its own "Licence to Deliver" TV spot.
Omega: luxury partner, ~29M views
Aston Martin — intertextual since Goldfinger

The 007.com website — why producers use it

  • Official information in one place — a trusted source; producers control the message (official news, not leaks).
  • Builds hype — trailers, posters, first-look images and countdowns before release.
  • Behind-the-scenes content — interviews and production features connect fans to the film.
  • Brand and franchise identity — the sleek design reflects Bond's luxury and sophistication; "The Bonds" page celebrates every era (nostalgia — think Uses & Gratifications: personal identity + entertainment for long-term fans).
  • Digital convergence — video, text, images, games and galleries all in one place.
  • Links ALL the marketing together — social media, ticket booking, partner promotions… and the 007 Store, making money from merchandise directly.
  • Global, 24/7 — reaches the international fanbase instantly; regular updates bring people back.
007.com homepage
"The Bonds" — nostalgia for every generation of fan
The store: merchandise revenue on-site

Convergence + synergy = the modern campaign

Synergy: two companies/brands connecting for mutual benefit — Omega sells watches, Bond gets a "real" spy kit and a co-funded ad campaign.

Technological convergence: we do everything on one device — so every product, poster and partner ad carries social links and hashtags (#NoTimeToDie). One click takes the audience from a partner's advert to the trailer to the ticket page.

Convergence makes synergy easy — and makes the whole campaign feel like one connected experience.

Merchandising

NTTD merchandise was marketed heavily on the official 007 Store — and the brand was licensed to other products, from branded cups to popcorn. Fans literally buy into the brand.

Licensed popcorn…
…and branded cups

Exam practice — the stepped question [17 marks, ~17 minutes]

Q3(a) Explain what high production values means [1] · (b) Development is the first stage of film production — give two other stages [2] · (c) Briefly explain the impact of production processes on film [4] · (d) Explain how No Time to Die is able to reach large, global audiences. Refer to its marketing campaign. [10]

(a) Having a large budget — a Hollywood blockbuster able to include lots of action scenes and CGI.

(b) Any two of: pre-production, production, post-production, distribution.

(c) Built-in fans of Daniel Craig, the other stars and the director; heavy use of real stunts increases costs but raises quality; filming for IMAX adds spectacle and revenue.

(d) A well-known hero with universal appeal and a simple good-vs-evil plot; a variety of trailers featuring global stars; social media and convergence via the 007.com website linking everything together; promotional partners (Omega, Aston Martin, adidas, Nokia…) extending the campaign to new audiences; worldwide locations pulling in audiences from those regions; a Royal Premiere streamed on YouTube for global publicity.

🌐 The Official Website — 007.com

You've seen above why producers use 007.com. Here it is as an exam-ready checklist — the eight jobs an official website does at once — applied to 007.com:

  • 1. A central hub — news, the films, cast information and trailers for the whole franchise in one place
  • 2. Maintains interest between releases — anniversary features and "Bond is back" news keep fans engaged in the long gaps between films
  • 3. Targets different audience segments — sections for the films, the novels, music and merchandise
  • 4. Generates revenue — the 007 Store sells merchandise and the site drives cinema-ticket and streaming sales
  • 5. Collects audience data — a newsletter sign-up builds a mailing list of Bond fans for targeted marketing
  • 6. Links to social media — links out to the official 007 Instagram, YouTube, Facebook and X
  • 7. Promotes synergy & brand partnerships — showcases product-placement partners such as Omega, Aston Martin, Nokia and Bollinger
  • 8. Gives producers control over brand image — EON and the producers control the official imagery and narrative, protecting the Bond brand (unlike reviews or social media)

09

Exam-Style Practice

For the Bond posters, the likely media language areas are: narrative [5] · genre [10] · colour [5] · images [5] · layout & design [5] · character roles · intertextuality. Representation comes as the 25-mark comparison with an unseen text.

How the questions have looked

  • "Explore how The Man with the Golden Gun film poster creates meanings through the use of: (a) colour [5] (b) genre conventions [10]"
  • 2023: "How does this film poster for Spectre communicate meaning? (a) narrative [5] (b) genre [10]"
  • Practice format: "Explore how the film poster uses codes and conventions. Analyse: (a) character roles [10] (b) narrative [5]"

Exam tips: you get a clean copy of the set text · no intro or conclusion needed for ML questions — get straight into analysis with clear connotations · know all the possible bullet-point areas · a solid paragraph with 2–3 pieces of evidence per bullet.

Q1 · "Explore how the TMWTGG poster uses codes and conventions: (a) character roles [10]"

Bond as the conventional "hero" and the unseen character holding the gun as the conventional "villain" (Propp). Bond's centrality and dominance reflect his importance and power; his dress codes connote professionalism and status; his direct mode of address makes him seem serious, intense, in control, trustworthy, calm. The "Bond women" take the conventional role of objects of desire — Propp's "princesses" who need saving — linked to their position in the frame, their gesture codes and dress codes. Minor characters: the henchmen, and the female kung-fu character mid-frame, positioned with Bond as a Proppian "helper" perhaps.

Q2 · "…(b) narrative [5]"

The conventional narrative of the hero in danger, connoted by the golden gun aimed directly at Bond; connotations of gold linked to status; conventional enigma codes around the unseen villain — who is trying to kill Bond, and where is the threat from? Conventional action codes (stunts, destruction, explosions) plus the roles each female character plays in the suggested narratives (one pointing at Bond, one with her arm across him).

Q3 · "…(c) intertextuality"

Producers' and Roger Moore's names positioned conventionally at the top, creating intertextuality with earlier Bonds and The Saint. Conventional "Bondian" iconography: dress codes, the gun, the 007 logo, exotic locations. Gold in the title links to Goldfinger, which established the franchise's codes. The kung-fu characters link to the 1970s popularity of martial arts films. The author's name before the title links to the original novel; the United Artists logo links to their other film properties.

Q4 · The 25-marker: "Compare the representation of gender in the two film posters" [25]

You must consider: producers' choices · how far the representations are similar · how far they are different. Spend ~10 minutes analysing the unseen text first. Structure: Intro → P1 rep in the set text → P2 rep in the unseen → P3 similarities → P4 differences → Conclusion.

Level 5 requires: detailed analysis of both texts focused on representation · detailed comparisons · consistent use of representation theory (stereotypes, patriarchal ideology, the male gaze) · terminology (representation, sexist, sexualised, connotation, composition, tagline, anchorage, typography, serif/sans-serif).

Starters: "One way gender is shown in the poster is through the use of… (costume/pose/colour/facial expression/camera angle)." · "In both posters, men/women are shown as…" · "However, in the first poster women are shown as… whereas in the second they are…"

Intro model: "The representations of men and women are stereotypical in comparison to today, as context in the 1970s poster reflects patriarchal ideology." Band 5 judgement: "Despite social change such as greater ethnic representation in NTTD, we could still argue some stereotypical representations are upheld."

Compare/contrast vocabulary: similar to, likewise, equally, in the same way · however, on the other hand, in contrast to, unlike, whereas.

Q5 · Contexts 5-marker: "Explain how contexts influence film posters. Refer to No Time to Die." [5]

Starters: "The female characters are shown as/with… to show changing roles for women today." · "The poster includes characters of different ethnic backgrounds to show that…" · "However, there are still some typical representations of women such as… this shows society has not fully…"
